title: Teaching himself to read, arrange and memorize
summary: Apart from about ten lessons in Jacksonville he was self-taught; he explains how he learned clefs, memorized scores by sight and wanted to write.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Well, just to -- digress one more time, when you say you taught yourself. You -- you can arrange, can't you?
Yeah.
Well did you end up teaching yourself how to arrange?
Yeah.
You did?
Uh-huh.
How -- I mean how early on were you able to write music, then?
Oh --
I mean how long did -- how many years were you working before you could actually sit down and write music? Write arrangements and things, cause that --
Oh, write arrangements?
Well I mean that means getting to know the voicing of all the different instruments and everything.
Well I guess --
It guess after you had the band awhile, huh?

Well, let me explain it this way. The way I got into writing, more or less, was when I started to play with four hammers, and it all goes in a number of years later (unintelligible), I'm getting ahead of myself --
Yes, I know --
-- but I started to try to play piano. Course I knew from the -- when I was six years old, I knew the keys of the piano --
Yeah.
-- I knew the -- I knew the different between a treble and bass clefs, so I taught myself the difference --
Yeah.
-- so I could recognize it, and so I got to reading it --
Yeah, I -- see.

And I -- I got so actually I could take a piece of music on the train and memorize it, by sight. I used to memorize the numbers that way. I'd take a 32-bar thing and look -- I still do. I can take it --
That's it -- that's it.
-- I can look at it by sight, and memorize it --
You've got a photographic memory, then?
And go and play it that night. And memorize the changes by watching it, looking at it.
Fancy that?
